plain_english: Difficult situations reveal who you really are. So when trouble hits you, remember that God is like a wrestling coach who pairs you with a tough opponent. Why does he do this? So you can become a champion. But you can't win without breaking a sweat. I think no one has ever been given a better opportunity than the difficulty you're facing right now — if you choose to handle it like an athlete handles a strong opponent.
original_excerpt: It is circumstances (difficulties) which show what men are. Therefore when a difficulty falls upon you, remember that God, like a trainer of wrestlers, has matched you with a rough young man. For what purpose? you may say. Why, that you may become an Olympic conqueror; but it is not accomplished without sweat. In my opinion no man has had a more profitable difficulty than you have had, if you choose to make use of it as an athlete would deal with a young antagonist.
source_reference: Discourses, How We Should Struggle with Circumstances

plain_english: Say we send a scout to Rome. No one sends a coward who panics at every little noise and shadow, then runs back screaming that the enemy is coming. So if you come to us saying, "Things are terrible in Rome! Death is awful! Exile is awful! Being insulted is awful! Being poor is awful! Run, friends — the enemy is near!" we'll tell you: "Get out of here. Keep your prophecies to yourself. Our only mistake was sending a scout like you."
original_excerpt: We are now sending a scout to Rome; but no man sends a cowardly scout, who, if he only hears a noise and sees a shadow anywhere, comes running back in terror and reports that the enemy is close at hand. So now if you should come and tell us: "Fearful is the state of affairs at Rome; terrible is death; terrible is exile; terrible is calumny; terrible is poverty; fly, my friends, the enemy is near," we shall answer: "Begone, prophesy for yourself; we have committed only one fault, that we sent such a scout."
source_reference: Discourses, How We Should Struggle with Circumstances

plain_english: Diogenes went ahead as a scout and came back with a different report. He says death is not evil because it's not shameful. He says fame is just crazy people making noise. And what did this scout say about pain, pleasure, and poverty? He says being naked is better than wearing fancy purple robes. Sleeping on bare ground is the softest bed. He proves each claim by pointing to his own courage, his peace of mind, his freedom, and his strong, healthy body. "There's no enemy nearby," he says. "Everything is peaceful." How can you say that, Diogenes? "Look," he replies, "have I been hit? Have I been wounded? Have I run away from anyone?" This is what a scout should be like. But you come to us telling us one scary thing after another. Go back and look again. You'll see more clearly once you stop being afraid.
original_excerpt: Diogenes, who was sent as a scout before you, made a different report to us. He says that death is no evil, for neither is it base; he says that fame (reputation) is the noise of madmen. And what has this spy said about pain, about pleasure, and about poverty? He says that to be naked is better than any purple robe, and to sleep on the bare ground is the softest bed; and he gives as a proof of each thing that he affirms his own courage, his tranquillity, his freedom, and the healthy appearance and compactness of his body. There is no enemy near, he says; all is peace. How so, Diogenes? "See," he replies, "if I am struck, if I have been wounded, if I have fled from any man." This is what a scout ought to be. But you come to us and tell us one thing after another. Will you not go back, and you will see clearer when you have laid aside fear?
source_reference: Discourses, How We Should Struggle with Circumstances
